transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Price (Redwood AE), Aisha Khan (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (CartaHealth Head of ML), Ethan Chen (Product), Priya Raman (Security)
Shared: https://redwood.co/poc/cartahealth/benchmarks-03-12 (benchmarks spreadsheet), slides (deck v5)

Summary (auto): quick pass on quality regressions after last week's prompt tuning; discussed scoring mismatches, guardrail false positives, and next steps for red-team + latency check on Dedicated.

[00:00] Jordan: All right, hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check, is the time still good for you all?
[00:07] Maya: yes, thanks Jordan. we've got—uh—about 45–60 min, sounds good.
[00:12] Ethan: yep good here.
[00:15] Jordan: cool. I'll hand off to Aisha to run through the latest results from prompt v2 -> v3 and the regression checks.
[00:22] Aisha: okay, cool. so we ran the 1k prompt set you shared last week, and the high-level is: overall pass rate improved from 72% to 81% on our internal rubric, but some categories regressed.
[00:35] Aisha: the examples that regressed are mostly tight clinical guidance prompts where the model hallucinated medication relationships — we saw a spike in confident-but-wrong answers.
[00:47] Maya: right, that's the big worry for us, safety/perf. did you see any pattern by prompt length or temperature?
[00:55] Aisha: mostly shorter prompts with a high directive, e.g., "summarize patient allergy risk" style prompts—when we increased instruction-following weight the model started to hypothesize absent data. temperature unchanged; this looks like an output-synthesis change due to the new few-shot templates.
[01:20] Jordan: and the scoring — remind me, you used combined metrics? rouge-ish + factuality?
[01:26] Aisha: we used the scoring pipeline we shared in the sheet: token-overlap (ROUGE-L), embedding-similarity + a factuality classifier we run as a pass/fail. combined score threshold is 0.65. a lot of the regressed items fail the factuality classifier despite decent overlap.
[01:45] Maya: hmm, that classifier's pretty sensitive to hallucination style. do you have the false positive rate?
[01:50] Aisha: on our tuned test split it's about 8% FPR, but on your domain subset it jumps to ~17%. could be domain mismatch.
[02:05] Priya: quick sec — on the logging front, are we keeping full prompts in the logs or redacting PHI? we need to confirm for compliance.
[02:13] Jordan: good point. for the POC we are storing request/response with redaction turned on by default; raw logs are behind a KMS envelope and we can set a 30 day retention. we'll send the config.
[02:30] Priya: ok please send the retention and KMS notes. also want to see the SOC2/ISO snippets for the Dedicated node since we may move to reserved infra.
[02:40] Jordan: yes we'll attach the security + compliance pack.

[02:55] Aisha: back to quality — we also ran guardrail ruleset v1 which rejects hallucinations based on entity mismatch and policy heuristics. it caught ~60% of hallucination cases but created false positives in templated summaries.
[03:12] Ethan: false positives how bad — are we losing useful outputs?
[03:15] Aisha: sometimes the guardrail rejects a valid synthesized recommendation because the heuristic expects a citation field; we can tune to be less strict for summary prompts.
[03:28] Maya: can we show a couple of examples?
[03:30] Aisha: yes — pulling up the sheet — example 347: prompt "given x, recommend med Y" — model suggested an off-label dose. guardrail flagged because dosage not in guideline DB — that's good, but it also flagged example 412 where model gave a safe paraphrase.
[03:55] Maya: ok so we'd prefer guardrails to err on the side of pass for non-actionable summaries, but block if the model suggests a prescriptive dose or diagnosis.
[04:07] Aisha: understood — we'll add a classification to route outputs: "actionable" vs "informational" and apply stricter checks on the actionable path.

[04:25] Jordan: on the prompt side we shipped v3 this morning which adds more negative examples and a short explicit refusal template. that moved some cases back into pass but introduced the hallucination spike I mentioned earlier.
[04:40] Maya: negative examples helped in many open prompts, though the dosage issue is still worrisome.
[04:46] Ethan: curious — what's the latency impact when we enable the factuality classifier and guardrail heuristics inline?
[04:52] Aisha: good question. running the classifier inline increases p95 latency by ~80–120ms on the hosted endpoint. on Dedicated we can offload to an async pipeline or run a lighter-weight embedding check to keep p95 < 600ms.
[05:12] Priya: what's your observed token cost increase with the new prompts?
[05:16] Aisha: token usage is up ~9% due to longer system instructions and few-shot examples. we have some quantization profiles that can reduce cost ~12% if you want to test.

[05:30] Jordan: I want to call out one regression type we saw — prompt injection where the model replies with content pulled from the few-shot that references internal examples. sometimes the model echoes bracketed placeholders.
[05:44] Maya: we've seen that too. our engineers flagged a template leak in two examples where PHI placeholders persisted.
[05:51] Aisha: we added a post-process scrubber for bracketed tokens but it's heuristic; we'll tighten that and add a test to the CI set.

[06:08] Aisha: ok next, scoring mismatches: we had 24 items where human score disagreed with our automated label — mostly because the human judged the tone or empathy, which our automatic pipeline doesn't capture.
[06:24] Maya: empathy matters a lot for patient-facing text. can we surface a separate sentiment/empathy metric? even a simple classifier or rule would help triage.
[06:33] Aisha: yes we can add a sentiment/empathy tag. it'll be a cheap model — embedding + logistic reg — and we'll add it to the sheet.

[06:50] Jordan: timeline/ask — we asked for 100 targeted regression examples from you, Maya, last week, and you sent 42. what's the blocker to getting the rest?
[07:00] Maya: the extraction from production is gated by privacy review; we'll push another batch by end of week but likely redacted.
[07:10] Priya: we need to make sure the shared examples are de-identified and there's an audit trail.
[07:15] Jordan: understood, we'll accept redacted examples. please include the redaction mapping notes in the upload.

[07:30] Ethan: about metrics, can we get an export of the scoring distribution? the sheet only has summary rows.
[07:36] Aisha: yes, full export is in the bench sheet; link is in the GH issue. I'll pull a filtered CSV for you after the call.

[07:50] Jordan: on the risk side, Priya, anything else we should know before scheduling Dedicated tests?
[07:55] Priya: two things — 1) KMS key ownership: we prefer customer-managed keys for Dedicated; 2) network egress: need a VPC peering diagram and ingress rules.
[08:06] Jordan: we have both — I'll attach the VPC peering doc and the Dedicated security checklist.

[08:20] Aisha: demo time — quick live examples. I'll run three prompts: a baseline, v2, and v3. please call out differences.
[08:28] (screenshare noise)
[08:32] [09:00] Aisha: baseline answer: "...patient may be at increased risk..." (acceptable).
[09:10] [09:38] Aisha: v2: added few-shot yielded slightly more concrete recommendation, still cautious.
[09:45] [10:12] Aisha: v3: tends to give a confident suggestion with phrasing like "recommended dose X" for some templates — that's the regression we flagged.
[10:25] Maya: that's exactly the pattern; we need a hard refusal for prescriptive language where data isn't present.
[10:32] Aisha: we'll augment the refusal template to explicitly say uncertain and ask for more data.

[10:45] Jordan: operational note — do you want us to run a nightly job that flags any new regressions and emails the team?
[10:52] Maya: yes please. daily digest would be great.
[10:55] Jordan: ok we'll wire that up to the bench sheet alerts.

[11:05] Aisha: technical detail — we enabled prefix caching on some routes which improved median latency by 20ms and reduced tokens by ~4% for repeated patient-summary flows. however cache invalidation is tricky for patient-specific data; we keep per-patient keys.
[11:28] Priya: confirm that cached outputs are encrypted and not accessible cross-account.
[11:33] Aisha: yes, per-tenant encryption and access controls; we'll include the config snippet.

[11:50] Jordan: ok let's capture the concrete next experiments: 1) prompt v3 + stricter refusal templates; 2) apply route-level guardrail tuning (actionable vs informational); 3) add empathy metric; 4) run Dedicated latency/cost check.
[12:10] Maya: will you also send the red-team checklist? we want to run internal adversarial prompts.
[12:15] Jordan: yep we'll share our red-team seed list and you can add domain-specific probes.

[12:30] Ethan: quick procurement note — if we move to Dedicated, what's typical lead time?
[12:35] Jordan: for reserved capacity it's ~2–3 weeks to provision initial Dedicated pool once contract signed; there's a quick onboarding checklist.

[12:45] Priya: ok last question on data retention — will logs for POC be retained 30 days by default?
[12:50] Jordan: yes 30 days default; can extend to 90 with a retention add-on.

[12:58] Jordan: great — recap and action items: we'll send prompt v3 artifacts, bench CSV, security pack, and schedule Dedicated perf run. Maya will push more redacted examples.
[13:12] Maya: thanks everyone.
[13:15] Jordan: thanks, bye.

Recap (auto): prompts v3 improved overall pass rate but introduced prescriptive hallucinations. Guardrails catch many but need nuanced tuning to avoid false positives. Immediate next steps: share artifacts, add empathy metric, run red-team + Dedicated latency test.
